name: Triamterene
lead: Triamterene is a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks epithelial sodium channels in the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the kidney, increasing sodium and water excretion while limiting potassium loss. It is used for edema and hypertension, most often in a fixed combination with hydrochlorothiazide. [1][2]

It appears on the wiki under depuffing because it is a diuretic. No published study has tested triamterene for facial puffiness or any cosmetic purpose, and no community discussion of it was available to document. [1]
Its US label carries a boxed warning about hyperkalemia, which can be fatal if uncorrected, and triamterene has also been linked to crystal-induced kidney injury. [2][3]

paras: Grokipedia describes triamterene as indicated for edema in heart failure, cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome, and for hypertension, alone or in fixed-dose combinations. [1] The US label for the triamterene and hydrochlorothiazide combination states it is not for initial therapy of edema or hypertension, but for patients who develop low potassium on hydrochlorothiazide alone or in whom low potassium cannot be risked. [2]

Triamterene blocks epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the late distal tubule and collecting duct, reducing the electrochemical gradient that drives potassium secretion and thus conserving potassium. [1]

The boxed warning states that abnormal potassium elevation can occur with all potassium-conserving diuretic combinations, is more likely in renal impairment, diabetes, and elderly or severely ill patients, and may be fatal if uncorrected, so frequent monitoring is advised. [2] Other labelled reactions include gastrointestinal effects, jaundice, pancreatitis and drowsiness. [2]

A 1999 review lists triamterene among drugs associated with crystals insoluble in urine that can cause acute renal failure. [3] A 2000 study of folic acid antagonists, a group that includes triamterene, examined associations with birth defects. [4]
No studies found on triamterene for facial puffiness or cosmetic depuffing. Clinical research concerns hypertension and edema.

The European Working Party on High Blood Pressure in the Elderly trial randomised 840 patients over 60 to hydrochlorothiazide plus triamterene or placebo and reported on mortality and morbidity. [5] The same group reported on glucose intolerance during diuretic therapy. [6]

timeline.event: US FDA approval, according to Grokipedia. [1]
European Working Party trial on mortality and morbidity with hydrochlorothiazide plus triamterene published. [5]

card.summary: A potassium-sparing diuretic for edema and hypertension; no study has tested it for facial puffiness, and its label warns of fatal hyperkalemia.

quick.overview:
Triamterene is a prescription potassium-sparing diuretic, usually taken with hydrochlorothiazide, for fluid retention and high blood pressure.

It is catalogued under depuffing as a diuretic, but no research addresses facial puffiness or appearance.
quick.mechanism: It blocks sodium channels in the final part of the kidney's tubules, so more sodium and water leave in urine while potassium is retained.
quick.risks: The US label carries a boxed warning that high potassium can be fatal if uncorrected, especially with kidney disease, diabetes or older age. Crystal-related kidney injury and gastrointestinal and liver effects are also reported. It is prescription-only.
